title: 2. Sub-Industry Mix & Constituent Revenue Engines

epigraph.quote: Every sub-industry inside XLV monetizes a different link in the patient care chain—from the molecule in the vial to the surgical robot in the operating room and the insurance card in the wallet.
epigraph.author: Healthcare Sector Underwriting Note

web_blocks.html: As of November 20, 2026, XLV holds 61 securities (tracking the 60-stock Health Care Select Sector Index plus cash/derivatives), with the top 10 constituents accounting for 60.64% of total fund assets [1][7]. This creates a barbell: mega-cap pharmaceutical and biotechnology innovators drive roughly 57.36% of the fund, while managed care, medical devices, and life sciences tools supply the remaining 42.02% [1].

web_blocks.text: 2.2 Real-World Unit Mechanics Across Every Sub-Industry

web_blocks.html: 1. Pharmaceuticals (37.15% weight): Consider a patient with obesity and type 2 diabetes visiting an endocrinologist. The physician prescribes Eli Lilly's weekly tirzepatide injection (Zepbound/Mounjaro) or its newly launched daily oral GLP-1 pill, Foundayo [17][18]. The patient's commercial insurer or Medicare Part D plan (via Lilly's Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program, which added 500,000+ fills since July 2026) reimburses the pharmacy at a negotiated net price after rebates [17]. Lilly books gross-to-net revenue—growing FY2025 sales 43% to $65.18 billion on 50% volume growth despite a 6% realized price decline—while earning an 84%–86% non-GAAP gross margin because chemical/peptide synthesis scales far faster than marginal manufacturing cost [16][17].

2. Biotechnology (20.21% weight): Unlike small-molecule pills, large-molecule biologics are grown inside living cell cultures and are harder to replicate. Take a patient with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis or Crohn's disease prescribed AbbVie's Skyrizi (risankizumab), or an HIV patient taking Gilead's Biktarvy. Rather than facing an abrupt 90% generic price collapse overnight, biologics enjoy 12-year U.S. regulatory exclusivity and complex biosimilar manufacturing barriers, generating recurring high-margin infusions or self-injections billed through specialty pharmacies.

3. Health Care Providers & Services (16.12% weight): Picture a 72-year-old retiree enrolling in a UnitedHealthcare Medicare Advantage plan [19]. CMS pays UnitedHealthcare a risk-adjusted monthly capitation fee per member. UnitedHealth must pay all hospital, physician, and pharmacy claims out of that fixed premium—its Medical Care Ratio (MCR, 88.4% in Q3 2026) [19]. Simultaneously, its Optum subsidiary operates outpatient clinics, pharmacy benefit management (OptumRx), and health-data analytics, capturing service fees while attempting to steer patients toward lower-cost ambulatory care.

4. Health Care Equipment & Supplies (15.48% weight): Walk into a hospital operating room where a surgeon performs a prostatectomy or cardiac valve repair using Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci 5 robotic system [24]. Intuitive sells or leases the capital system upfront ($1.5M–$2.5M), but the real economic engine is the razor-and-blade recurring stream: single-use robotic instruments, sterile drapes, and annual service contracts billed every time the robot operates—now exceeding 10,000 procedures per day globally at ~69% gross margins [24]. Similarly, Abbott sells a reusable reader/app alongside disposable FreeStyle Libre sensors replaced every 14 days.

5. Life Sciences Tools & Services (10.42% weight): Before any drug reaches a pharmacy, a biopharma lab must discover, test, and manufacture it. When a biotech scales a monoclonal antibody or GLP-1 peptide, it buys single-use bioreactor bags, chromatography resins, mass spectrometers, and contract-manufacturing (CDMO) capacity from Thermo Fisher Scientific or Danaher [23]. Thermo Fisher acts as the 'picks-and-shovels' supplier to the entire sector, generating $44.56 billion in FY2025 revenue (guided to $47.7B–$48.2B in FY2026) without taking binary Phase 3 clinical trial risk [23].

web_blocks.title: Why Sub-Industry Balance Matters
paragraphs: When hospital surgical volumes surge, Providers (UNH) face higher MCR claims costs, but Equipment makers (ISRG, ABT, SYK) and Pharma capture higher procedure and prescription volumes. XLV's multi-vertical structure creates natural internal hedging across the healthcare dollar.

web_blocks.text: 2.3 Geographic Revenue Footprint, Payer Mix & Health Care Technology (0.61%)

web_blocks.html: While XLV holds exclusively U.S.-listed S&P 500 companies, its look-through revenue base is deeply global. Mega-cap pharmaceutical and MedTech constituents such as Eli Lilly, Johnson & Johnson, Merck, and Intuitive Surgical generate roughly 35% to 48% of their revenue outside the United States across Europe, Japan, and emerging markets [16][20][22][24]. By contrast, Health Care Providers & Services (16.12% of XLV) are overwhelmingly domestic, tied to U.S. commercial employer plans, Medicare Advantage, and Medicaid reimbursement [1][19]. This split provides natural currency and regulatory diversification: U.S. domestic managed-care margin pressure does not impair international medical-device or specialty-pharma demand.

The smallest GICS slice inside XLV—Health Care Technology at 0.61%—comprises healthcare IT, clinical workflow software, and electronic health record infrastructure [1]. Though minor in weight today, software-enabled revenue-cycle management and AI-assisted clinical documentation increasingly interface with the Providers and Life Sciences verticals, improving prior-authorization turnaround times and clinical-trial patient recruitment across XLV's larger constituents [19][23].

web_blocks.text: 2.4 Gross-to-Net Pricing, Rebates & Sub-Industry Margin Dispersion

web_blocks.html: A critical nuance inside XLV's constituent revenue engines is the divergence between list prices and realized net prices. In Pharmaceuticals (37.15% weight) and Biotechnology (20.21% weight), manufacturers negotiate confidential rebates with pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) such as OptumRx, CVS Caremark, and Express Scripts [1][17][19]. Eli Lilly's FY2025 results illustrate the trade-off: realized U.S. prices declined 6% (and 9% in Q2 2026), yet 50%–60% volume growth drove revenue up 43% to $65.18B and lifted non-GAAP gross margins to 86.3% [16][17]. Conversely, legacy franchises facing biosimilar entry—such as Johnson & Johnson's Stelara—experienced -3.1% net pricing headwinds that trimmed consolidated gross margin by 120 bps to 67.9% [22].

Downstream Wholesaler Concentration (Blind-Spot Audit): Beyond PBM rebates, XLV's pharmaceutical and biotech constituents (57.36% of fund assets) rely heavily on an oligopoly of three U.S. wholesale distributors—McKesson (1.94% of XLV), Cencora, and Cardinal Health. Eli Lilly's FY2025 Form 10-K confirms that each of these three distributors accounted for a significant percentage of consolidated revenue across 2023–2025 [16]. Because XLV holds both the drugmakers and the wholesalers inside the same sector basket, wholesaler fee-for-service renegotiations, inventory destocking, or distributor credit/regulatory disruptions transmit directly across multiple sub-industries.

340B Drug Discount Drag (Blind-Spot Audit): Drug makers in XLV (57.36% weight) also face growing discounts under the federal 340B program. HRSA data from July 2026 show discounted 340B hospital drug purchases jumped 23% YoY to $100.0 billion in CY2025, up from $81.4 billion in 2024 and $53.7 billion in 2022 [40]. At list prices, those drugs topped $180 billion, creating about $79.5 billion in steep discounts [40]. Twenty-one states now bar drug makers from capping contract-pharmacy sales, and HRSA set a new 340B rebate pilot to start January 1, 2027 [40]. This steady cash-flow leak sits right next to commercial PBM rebates and trims real pharma margins.

book_paragraphs: To understand what you actually own inside XLV, forget ticker symbols for a moment and follow a single patient through the American healthcare system. Every dollar spent on that patient's care flows into one of five distinct business models—and XLV owns the market-leading tollbooth in all five.

When you and I look at the Nov 2026 holdings sheet, 60.38% of your capital sits in just ten companies, and 37.15% sits in Pharmaceuticals alone. Yet the remaining 63% across Biotechnology, Providers, Medical Equipment, and Life Sciences Tools is what keeps XLV from behaving like a one-note drug bet.

Let us look even closer at the economic diversity hiding inside those six GICS industries. On paper, healthcare sounds like one monolithic sector. In reality, you own six distinct business models with completely different margin profiles, capital intensities, and customer relationships. A pharmaceutical patent holder sells a chemical or biologic molecule at an 85% gross margin to wholesalers and pharmacy benefit managers. A medical-device manufacturer sells a multi-million-dollar surgical robot to a hospital CFO, then collects a high-margin toll every time a surgeon scrubs in.

Meanwhile, a managed-care insurer operates like a regulated utility crossed with an actuarial risk pool: it collects fixed monthly premiums from employers and the federal government, then manages a sprawling network of hospitals, doctors, and pharmacies to keep medical claims below 89 cents on the dollar. And sitting underneath all of them are the life-sciences toolmakers—the companies selling the mass spectrometers, sterile single-use bioreactor bags, and contract-research capacity that every drug developer needs whether their Phase 3 trial succeeds or fails.

There is also a hidden distribution bottleneck inside XLV that most sector summaries skip: customer concentration among the Big Three U.S. pharmaceutical wholesalers—McKesson (1.94% of XLV), Cencora, and Cardinal Health. As Eli Lilly discloses in its FY2025 Form 10-K, each of those three distributors accounts for a significant share of consolidated revenue. Because XLV owns both the drug innovators and the wholesalers in one wrapper, channel destocking or fee-for-service disputes ripple across both sides of the portfolio.

Alongside wholesaler concentration sits a second gross-to-net friction that rarely makes headline ETF summaries: the federal 340B Drug Pricing Program. HRSA reported that discounted 340B hospital and safety-net purchases surged 23% to $100.0 billion in 2025—doubling in five years and exceeding $180 billion before discounts. As twenty-one states block manufacturer contract-pharmacy limits and HRSA prepares its January 2027 rebate pilot, 340B leakage quietly compresses net realizations across XLV's pharmaceutical and biotech leaders.

book_subsections.title: Five Tollbooths on the Healthcare Dollar
paragraphs: Start in the research lab: Thermo Fisher sells the mass spectrometers, single-use bioreactor bags, and clinical-trial logistics that every drugmaker needs regardless of which molecule wins FDA approval. Move to the pharmacy counter: Eli Lilly, Merck, AbbVie, and Johnson & Johnson monetize patent-protected intellectual property at 70%–86% gross margins, trading decades of R&D risk for blockbuster cash flows.

Then step into the operating room and the insurer's actuarial desk. Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci 5 systems run over 10,000 procedures a day, locking in recurring instrument revenue per surgery. Meanwhile, UnitedHealth Group collects monthly premiums for 48.3 million members and tries to keep medical claims near 88 cents on the dollar. Notice the built-in tension: when seniors undergo more surgeries, Intuitive wins and UnitedHealth's Medical Care Ratio ticks up. Inside XLV, those opposing forces partially cancel each other out.

book_subsections.title: How the Patient Dollar Flows Through All Six Verticals
paragraphs: Walk through a real-world example so you can see these cash flows interact. Imagine a fifty-eight-year-old patient diagnosed with obesity, sleep apnea, and early-stage osteoarthritis. At the primary-care visit, their insurer—say UnitedHealth Group—processes the claim. If the physician prescribes Eli Lilly's tirzepatide or oral Foundayo, Lilly books the high-margin product revenue, while UnitedHealth's OptumRx pharmacy benefit manager negotiates rebates and manages fulfillment.

If that same patient later requires a knee or robotic soft-tissue procedure, Intuitive Surgical or Stryker supplies the operating-room hardware and disposable instruments, while Abbott's diagnostic or continuous-monitoring sensors track recovery. And behind the scenes, Thermo Fisher Scientific supplied the analytical instruments and bioproduction consumables used to manufacture the biologic or peptide therapy in the first place. When you hold XLV, you are not betting on one link in that chain—you own the entire U.S. clinical ecosystem.

book_subsections.title: Understanding Gross-to-Net Economics Across the Healthcare Chain
paragraphs: One of the biggest mistakes outside investors make when analyzing healthcare is confusing a drug's headline list price with the net revenue a company actually books. Every branded prescription passes through a complex rebate negotiation between manufacturers, pharmacy benefit managers, and commercial or Medicare insurers.

Watch how differently that plays out inside XLV. Eli Lilly willingly accepted 6% to 9% net price declines on tirzepatide in exchange for broad formulary access, unlocking 50% to 60% volume growth that pushed non-GAAP gross margins to 86.3%. Meanwhile, Johnson & Johnson absorbed -3.1% net pricing pressure as Stelara faced biosimilars, nudging its gross margin down 1.2 percentage points to 67.9%. When you own XLV, you own both sides of that gross-to-net negotiation—the innovators gaining volume share and the PBMs administering the rebates.

book_subsections.title: Why Eli Lilly's 16.81% Weight Is Both an Engine and a Concentration Watch
paragraphs: When you look at XLV's top-ten list, one number jumps off the page immediately: Eli Lilly at 16.81% of the entire fund, followed by Johnson & Johnson at 10.01%, AbbVie at 7.79%, and Merck at 5.09%. Those four names alone represent nearly 40% of your capital. In a typical sector fund, having one company approach 17% of assets would make a conservative risk manager nervous.

Yet notice why that happened: Eli Lilly earned that weight through 43% revenue growth in FY2025, 50% to 60% GLP-1 volume expansion, and an 86% gross margin that no peer could match. Meanwhile, S&P Dow Jones Indices' quarterly 25/50 capping rule stands ready at the 23% single-stock buffer to trim Lilly automatically if its outperformance continues. You get the upside of the biggest secular volume wave in modern pharmaceuticals without letting single-stock risk run completely unchecked.

book_subsections.title: Why Sub-Industry Dispersion Is a Feature, Not a Bug
paragraphs: Whenever one vertical inside XLV hits an air pocket—just as Managed Care did this week on Medicare Advantage audit headlines—another vertical like GLP-1 pharmaceuticals or robotic surgery often picks up the slack. That internal handoff is why owning all six GICS healthcare industries inside one wrapper smooths out the ride compared to single-stock or single-vertical bets.

Keep that six-vertical architecture in mind as we move forward: Pharmaceuticals and Biotechnology supply the high-margin intellectual property engine, Providers manage patient risk pools and pharmacy networks, Medical Equipment delivers operating-room razor-and-blade annuities, and Life Sciences Tools sell the essential lab consumables—creating a balanced healthcare ecosystem inside one ticker.
